faq.q: Why is the eye of a hurricane calm?
faq.a: In the eye, air gently sinks from high up, which warms and dries it so clouds fade away. The spinning winds around it cannot reach the very centre, so winds there are light.
asks: What is the eye of a storm?

faq.q: Where are a hurricane's strongest winds?
faq.a: In the eyewall, the ring of towering storm clouds around the eye. Here air spirals inward fastest and rises, giving the most violent winds and heaviest rain.
Rainbands are long, curved bands of clouds and thunderstorms that spiral into the storm. They bring bursts of heavy rain and strong gusts, with calmer gaps between them.
asks: Why does hurricane rain come and go?

faq.a: Most hurricanes are a few hundred kilometres across, and the biggest can be over 1,000 kilometres wide. The calm eye in the middle is usually 30 to 65 kilometres across.

faq.q: Is it safe to go outside in the eye?
faq.a: No. The calm can last only minutes to an hour, then the other side of the eyewall arrives with violent winds from the opposite direction. Stay sheltered until the whole storm has passed.
asks: What happens after the eye passes?
